extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of early modern philosophy (readers of John Locke)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize Locke's substantive claims about ideas, substances, collective ideas, and relation as presented in these chapters; useful for philosophical commentary or peer review of Locke's arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific ideas of substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Our SPECIFIC ideas of substances are nothing else but A COLLECTION OF CERTAIN NUMBER OF SIMPLE IDEAS, CONSIDERED AS UNITED IN ONE THING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's exemplar: the idea 'swan' = white colour, long neck, red beak, black legs, whole feet, certain size, power of swimming and making a certain noise, etc. Emphasize that what we call the idea of a substance is a compound of sensible simple ideas united in one common subject; the 'substratum' itself remains obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of spiritual substances as clear as bodily substances
rubrics_metrics.description: By composing the simple ideas from reflection (thinking, understanding, willing, perceiving, power of beginning motion, etc.) we can frame the COMPLEX IDEA OF AN IMMATERIAL SPIRIT; this is 'as clear and distinct' as our idea of material substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues parity of clarity: putting together ideas of thinking, perceiving, liberty, and power of moving yields the notion of an immaterial spirit in the same way that coherent parts and power of motion yield matter. Use examples of composed mental operations to show parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: No idea of abstract substance
rubrics_metrics.description: We have no clear distinct idea of the substance (either body or spirit) itself; our ideas are limited to the complex of qualities (simple ideas) we receive from sensation and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke insists that inquiry beyond those simple ideas (to the 'real essence' or substratum) leads to darkness and ignorance; the supposed substratum is a 'I know not what'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary ideas peculiar to body
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary ideas PECULIAR TO BODY are the COHESION OF SOLID, AND CONSEQUENTLY SEPARABLE, PARTS, and a POWER OF COMMUNICATING MOTION BY IMPULSE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure (shape) is treated as consequent upon finite extension. These two properties (cohesion and impulse) are the foundation of our idea of material substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary ideas peculiar to spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas PECULIAR TO SPIRIT are THINKING, and WILL, or A POWER OF PUTTING BODY INTO MOTION BY THOUGHT, AND, WHICH IS CONSEQUENT TO IT, LIBERTY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke contrasts the passive nature of matter with the active motivity of minds; he treats volition and the power to begin/stop motion as defining mental attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence, duration, and mobility common to both
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas of EXISTENCE, DURATION, and MOBILITY are common to both body and spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are shared simple ideas that appear in complex ideas of both kinds of substances; mobility is claimed for finite spirits as well as bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirits are capable of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite spirits are as capable of change of place (motion) as bodies; Locke claims there is no reason to deny mobility to spirits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: spirits operate only where they are; the soul, when united to the body, changes place with it (e.g., during travel) and thus can be considered in motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: God immoveable because infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion cannot be attributed to God because he is infinite; the infinite spirit is not 'in loco' and so immobility follows from infinity, not merely immateriality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a special-case qualification about the divine infinite spirit, distinguished from finite spirits which can be conceived as movable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas of spirit and body are parallel constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Both our complex idea of BODY (AN EXTENDED SOLID SUBSTANCE, CAPABLE OF COMMUNICATING MOTION BY IMPULSE) and of SOUL (A SUBSTANCE THAT THINKS AND HAS A POWER OF EXCITING MOTION IN BODY) are formed by uniting simple ideas and are equally obscure regarding the substratum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke invites comparison to show neither is more intelligible in its ultimate nature; use this parity to critique appeals to 'more obviousness' of matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohesion of solid parts as conceptually difficult as thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding how solid parts cohere (what makes extension possible) is no less obscure than understanding how a thinking substance thinks; both resist further intelligible explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses empirical puzzles (fusion of metals, cohesion of atoms) to show gaps in mechanistic explanations of cohesion, arguing parity of mystery with mental phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambient fluid pressure does not intelligibly explain cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: The pressure of an ambient fluid (aether) cannot be an intelligible cause of cohesion because it would not resist lateral sliding and thus fails to account for cohesive strength in all modes of separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke offers a thought-experiment about lateral separation of surfaces to show limits of the ambient-pressure hypothesis; apply this as a critique of certain mechanistic accounts of cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohesion of atoms in extended substances incomprehensible
rubrics_metrics.description: The bonds or 'cement' that unify the smallest particles (atoms, corpuscles) into coherent solids is unknown and would still leave unexplained the cohesion of those bonds' parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even hypothesizing finer particles (aether) shifts the problem downward; emphasizes epistemic humility about ultimate physical constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication of motion by impulse and by thought equally unintelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Although experience furnishes clear evidence of motion produced by both impulse (bodies) and thought (minds), the manner of transfer or production in both cases is obscure to understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke stresses parity: both phenomena are empirically evident but metaphysically mysterious. Use this point to reject inferential asymmetry favoring mechanical explanations over mental causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active vs passive power distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Active power (motivity) is clearer in spirit than in body; bodies communicate motion by transferred impulse (passive reception), whereas minds exhibit an active power to move.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to conjecture about beings that are both active and passive (created spirits) and the special cases of pure spirit (only active) and pure matter (only passive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation and reflection set boundaries of our ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple ideas we receive from sensation and reflection are the boundaries of our thoughts; beyond them the mind cannot discover the true natures, causes, or the 'real essences' of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's methodological point: philosophical inquiry should respect epistemic limits given by origin of ideas; attempts to penetrate substrata lead to confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex idea of God constructed by enlarging simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Our complex idea of the Supreme Being is made by enlarging simple ideas of existence, knowledge, power, pleasure, duration, etc., to infinity (e.g., infinite knowledge, power, eternity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: take ideas from reflection/sensation and amplify their degree/extent to produce the notion of an infinite, eternal, omniscient/powerful being.

rubrics_metrics.name: No ideas in our complex ideas of spirits beyond sensation or reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Apart from 'infinity', there is no idea we attribute to God (or spirits) that is not originally part of our ideas gained from sensation or reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: we cannot form an idea of 'immediate communication' among spirits because we have no experience of it; thus some divine or spiritual attributes remain conceptually opaque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective ideas of substances
rubrics_metrics.description: A collective idea is one idea made up of many particular substances considered together (e.g., ARMY, WORLD); such collections are represented by the mind as single ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke treats collective ideas as analogous to complex ideas of single substances: unity of representation, regardless of multiplicity of constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective ideas formed by the mind's power of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind composes collective ideas by uniting several particular substances or ideas into one representation (just as it composes numbers or complex ideas of individuals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize mental 'power of composition'—the ability to aggregate diverse items under one conception or name (score, gross, troop, city, fleet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial composite things are collective ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Most artificial things made of distinct substances (e.g., army, constellation, universe) are collective ideas—artificial draughts of the mind bringing remote independent things into one conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These collective ideas are useful for thought and discourse though their constituents may be widely disparate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation arises from comparison of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation is an idea we get from comparing things one with another; when the mind considers one thing with reference to another it forms the idea of RELATION (or RESPECT) and denotes this by relative terms (relatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: husband (intimates another person), whiter (intimates something compared to). Any idea can be a foundation of relation; relations are derived, not intrinsic, in Locke's account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations without correlative terms are less evident
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations expressed by relative/correlative terms (father/son) are obvious, but where language lacks correlatives the relation may be less readily apprehended (e.g., 'concubine' in languages without a correlative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes linguistic contingency: the presence/absence of correlatives affects the recognition of relations; some denominative terms are 'external denominations'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seemingly absolute terms may conceal tacit relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some terms that appear absolute (OLD, GREAT, IMPERFECT) implicitly include relations and thus conceal a tacit relational aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke signals that apparent absolutes often involve implicit comparison or reference; he'll expand this in later chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation is distinct from the related things
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea of relation may be the same among people who have differing ideas of the related things (e.g., different conceptions of 'man' but agreement on 'father' as a relational notion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke treats relations as superinduced on substances or modes, referring only to acts or connections (e.g., begetting) rather than altering the positive nature of the related substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of relation can occur without change in the related things
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation may cease (or change) through alteration of the correlatum without any change in the subject itself (e.g., Caius ceases to be a father by his son's death though he himself remains unchanged).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that relations are dependent on external reference, not intrinsic features of the subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations involve two things; wholes may be absolute despite relative parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation presupposes at least two things compared; yet a composite whole (e.g., triangle) is a positive absolute idea even when its parts are considered in relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between the relativity of parts and the absolutness of the whole-idea produced by uniting parts into a single representation.
